drawdown_context: Casual-dining holding company (Outback, Carrabba's, Bonefish, Fleming's) trading at $8.81 on 2025-05-15 against a stock that started 2024 above $27 — roughly a 67% drawdown over ~17 months. FY24 was the worst year in years: negative U.S. comp sales (-1.1%), traffic -4.4%, operating margin compression (3.5% from 6.8%), GAAP net loss of $(128)M including a $162.6M Brazil disposal impairment. Brazil sale closed 12/30/2024 (Vinci Partners, ~$225M for 67% + $59.9M retained-interest fair value), CEO David Deno retired Sep 2024 and was replaced by Mike Spanos (ex-Delta COO, ex-Six Flags CEO, ex-PepsiCo). Dividend cut from $0.24/qtr to $0.15/qtr (-37.5%) declared Feb 2025; 17% Tampa HQ workforce reduction announced Feb 20, 2025; $96.8M repurchase authorization remained but zero buybacks Q4 2024 and Q1 2025 after $266M in 1H 2024 at ~$27/share (asymmetric buyback timing).

rfm_tuples.R: FY24 comparable restaurant sales by brand (U.S., continuing operations): Outback Steakhouse (1.2)%, Carrabba's Italian Grill 0.0%, Bonefish Grill (3.2)%, Fleming's Prime Steakhouse 0.2%, Combined U.S. (1.1)%. Decomposition: combined U.S. = traffic (4.4)% + check 3.3%. Brand-level traffic: Outback (4.2)%, Carrabba's (3.2)%, Bonefish (7.1)%, Fleming's (5.8)%.
rfm_tuples.f: Traffic-vs-price decomposition: assess whether 'roughly flat' headline combined comp masks pure traffic erosion. Test whether the 4.4% combined traffic decline can be sustained against the 3.3% check increase (which is itself decelerating from 4.5% in FY23).
rfm_tuples.M_value: Combined U.S. traffic -4.4% vs check +3.3% — yields headline -1.1%, BUT (a) every single brand had negative traffic and (b) Bonefish lost 7.1% of guests on top of 3.9% pricing — a brand that has now seen seven consecutive years of negative traffic in disclosed data (Q3'24 YTD traffic -6.7%, prior year -3.1%). Check growth decelerated from 4.5% to 3.3% YoY — the pricing lever is exhausting itself. Q1 2025 10-Q (filed 2025-05-08, pre-cutoff): Outback comp -1.3% (deteriorating from -1.2%), Bonefish -4.0% (deteriorating from -3.2% full year). Bonefish Q1'25 traffic -9.4% — catastrophic.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Headline combined U.S. comp -1.1% is technically modest, but the brand-by-brand decomposition shows: (1) all four brands have negative traffic, (2) Bonefish is structurally impaired (~$3.2K AUV vs ~$3.3K LY, -7.1% traffic, has been negative for years), (3) the pricing lever decelerated 120bps YoY and decelerated further in Q1'25. Pre-cutoff 10-Q confirms Outback and Bonefish continued to deteriorate in Q1'25 — Bonefish traffic at -9.4% Q1'25 is a brand in run-off. The 'asset improvements' and 'simplify the agenda' narrative is not arresting the traffic decline at the core brands.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Sale of Majority Ownership of our Brazil Operations - On December 30, 2024, we completed the sale of 67% of our Brazil operations.' Total enterprise valuation R$2.06B (~$336M); BLMN sold 67% for R$1.4B (~$225.3M USD on closing) with $103.9M paid 12/30/24 net of withheld taxes; second installment of 48% due 12/30/2025. Put/call window 10/1/2028–12/31/2028. Recorded $68.3M impairment to disposal group at Q4 2024 (driven by $212.2M cumulative CTA losses).
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-A existence + Mode-B economic test: (i) Brazil was BLMN's growth engine (FY24 disc-ops restaurant sales $525M = 14% of total system revenue, FY23 disc-ops comp +5.5% vs U.S. flat) — selling it is a strategic retreat, not 'asset-light' optimization. (ii) Test whether the $336M EV mark is full vs intrinsic value, and whether the implied trade is value-accretive net of (a) $68.3M impairment, (b) lower royalty rate on new franchise agreement vs historic 5% intercompany, (c) loss of 14% of system sales.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Aggregate consideration: $225.3M USD for 67% + $59.9M USD fair value for retained 33% = $285.2M implied EV before lost royalty income. Filing explicitly admits: 'we entered into franchise agreements ... that include royalty rates that are lower than our historical intercompany rates and on the low end of our international franchisee royalty percentage range.' Brazil disc-ops contributed Net income from disc ops of +$41.6M (FY23) and +$16.1M (FY22); FY24 disc ops Net loss $(76.0)M but only because of the $68.3M write-down — operating Brazil was profitable. Brazil was also growing units (173 vs 155 YoY).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: BLMN sold its only growing segment (Brazil: +5.5% FY23 comp, unit count growing 12% YoY) to a Vinci Partners fund and is left with a 100% domestic casual-dining business that is shrinking in both traffic (-4.4%) and units (73 U.S. closures in FY24). The $225M USD upfront proceeds went to revolver paydown, not strategic reinvestment. The retained 33% has a structured put-call window in 2028 at a 'defined multiple of earnings less net indebtedness' — meaning if Brazil compounds, BLMN largely doesn't capture it, and if it stumbles, BLMN owns 33% of a deteriorating asset. Strategic interpretation: this is forced de-leveraging dressed as 'simplification' — exactly the kind of disposal a distressed franchisor does to buy time on the balance sheet.

rfm_tuples.R: 'In February 2025, our Board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.15 per share, payable on March 26, 2025.' Dividend was $0.24/share in every quarter of FY24 (declared and paid $0.96 annual). New rate = $0.60 annual.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-A: dividend cut from $0.24 to $0.15 = 37.5% cut. Mode-B: cross-reference with covenant-distance and forward EPS to test whether cut was discretionary (capital allocation) or compelled (covenant proximity / Brazil JV indemnification reserves / 2025 Notes refinancing needs). Also: BLMN expressly says future dividends depend on 'continued compliance with our financial covenants.'
rfm_tuples.M_value: Dividend cut 37.5% on Feb 2025 declaration — done CONCURRENT with the 17% Tampa HQ workforce reduction announced Feb 20, 2025 (8-K) and concurrent with the FY24 10-K filing. The Q1 2025 dividend payment was only $12.7M vs $21.1M in Q1 2024 — saves ~$33-34M annualized. The 2025 Notes ($20.7M residual) matured May 1, 2025 (per 10-Q footnote, settled with revolver). New 5-year Credit Agreement signed 9/19/2024 ($1.2B revolver, TNLR ≤ 4.50x). FY24 cash from ops continuing $216M, capex $221M — already FCF negative before any return-of-capital.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Material dividend cut — the kind that, in the framework taxonomy, is itself a 'distress signal.' Context multiplies the signal: it's paired with a 17% HQ headcount cut, zero Q4'24/Q1'25 buybacks (after $266M in 1H 2024 at $27 average), the Brazil JV (forced de-leveraging), and a step-down in capex guidance from prior trajectory. Management did NOT clearly disclose this dividend cut alongside the 10-K MD&A narrative of 'returning excess cash to shareholders through dividends' — the cut was via separate Board declaration referenced in passing. This is the most reliable single signal in the file.

rfm_tuples.R: 'On March 1, 2024, the Company entered into an accelerated share repurchase agreement (the ASR Agreement) ... to repurchase $220.0 million of the Company's common stock. Under the ASR Agreement, the Company repurchased 7.9 million shares of common stock through April 23, 2024 ... at $27.13 average per share.' Q1 2024 buyback: 6.948M shares at $27.13 = $188.5M. Q2: 2.156M at $27.36. Q3: 0.969M at $18.78. Q4 2024: zero. Q1 2025: zero.
rfm_tuples.f: Capital allocation tell — asymmetric buyback timing relative to forward price. Pace ($188.5M in Q1 alone = 71% of full-year), trough avoidance (zero in Q3 collapse and Q4'24 / Q1'25), and the fact that the ASR was structured concurrent with the $83.6M 2025 Notes Partial Repurchase / 7.5M-share dilution from convertible settlement, makes this a textbook asymmetric pattern.
rfm_tuples.M_value: 10.07M shares repurchased FY24 at $26.38 weighted average; zero shares in Q4 2024 (price ~$15) and zero in Q1 2025 (price collapsed from ~$15 to ~$9). Average repurchase price ($26.38) is ~3x the May 2025 spot price (~$9). The ASR was funded with 'borrowings under the revolving credit facility and net cash from the 2024 Note Hedge Early Termination Agreements' — i.e., levered buyback at the cycle high. FY24 buyback $265.7M + dividends $82.6M = $348.3M total return against $216M continuing-ops cash from ops and -$5M free cash flow.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Classic late-cycle capital allocation error: $220M ASR executed at $27.13 (cycle peak) immediately before SSS turned negative, the 2025 Notes had to be refinanced, the CEO was replaced, and a 17% HQ headcount cut became necessary. Repurchases stopped completely once price collapsed — exactly when value-disciplined buybacks would accelerate. The $96.8M of remaining authorization (expires Aug 13, 2025) is dead capital. Capital return for FY24 exceeded operating cash flow by $132M; the gap was funded by revolver draw, materially worsening the leverage trajectory.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Michael Spanos ... Chief Executive Officer and member of the Board of Directors since September 2024 ... W. Michael Healy ... Chief Financial Officer ... since April 2024 ... Lissette Gonzalez ... Chief Commercial Officer since February 2025 ... Pat Hafner ... EVP, Outback Steakhouse since January 2025.' Prior CEO David Deno retired effective 9/3/2024; Outback President Brett Patterson resigned effective 9/27/2024. Concurrent with 8-K of 10/21/2024, Board approved Amended & Restated Severance Pay Plan adding Section 16 Executive Officers to scope.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B forensic: C-suite churn proximate to bad-news disclosures. New CEO (Sept 2024) + new CFO (April 2024) + new Outback President (Jan 2025) + new Carrabba's President (Feb 2025) + new Chief Commercial Officer (Feb 2025) + departure of Brett Patterson (Outback, Sept 2024) + departure of Brazil exec Pierre Berenstein (Dec 2024, to head Brazil JV) = essentially the entire C-suite has rotated in 12 months. The new severance plan adopted Oct 2024 with executive-officer scope expansion is a defensive retention mechanism timed precisely with CEO transition and pre-Q4 impairment.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Within ~12 months: 5 of ~7 named executive officers either newly appointed, newly promoted, or about to depart. Healy (CFO since April 2024) has tenure of ~10 months at 10-K filing — the 10-K is signed by both Spanos (CEO since Sept) and Healy (CFO since April). The Q1 2025 10-Q is signed by SVP/CAO Philip Pace, NOT by CFO Healy — a notable sub-cert in a quarter with declining margins. The Amended Severance Plan (Oct 21, 2024) explicitly added 'officers of the Company considered Executive Officers for purposes of Section 16' — i.e., the C-suite retention payments were enhanced just before the bad-news cycle.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The volume of C-suite change is extreme even for a turnaround context. The pattern — new CEO (with no restaurant operating background; Delta COO/Six Flags/PepsiCo), new CFO who came from internal supply-chain rotation (not finance pedigree), new operating presidents at every brand — is consistent with a board scrambling to engineer credibility while keeping the same operating playbook. The Q1 2025 10-Q sub-cert by the CAO rather than CFO is mildly anomalous and worth flagging. The Oct 2024 severance-plan expansion to Section 16 officers, right before the goodwill / impairment cycle, is the textbook 'defensive governance' pattern this framework targets.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Provision for impaired assets and restaurant closings ... $64.3M (FY24) vs $33.6M (FY23) vs $6.0M (FY22) ... Q4 2024 Restaurant Impairment - During the thirteen weeks ended December 29, 2024, the Company recorded asset impairment charges of $25.5 million primarily related to 41 older, underperforming U.S. restaurants ... The projections considered, among other factors, continued challenging operating and macroeconomic conditions since these restaurants tend to underperform Company-wide averages for sales and operating income.' Goodwill carrying value $213.3M, trade names $414.7M.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B: derive forward impairment risk. Test the consistency between (a) Q4 2024 $25.5M impairment on 41 stores (~$622K avg) + 73 store closures since 12/25/22 vs (b) management's assertion of no goodwill impairment based on Q2 2024 qualitative test. Outback (largest brand) has the largest goodwill bucket implicitly; SSS continues to decline.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Impairment provision compounded from $6.0M (FY22) → $33.6M (FY23) → $64.3M (FY24) = ~10x in two years. Q4 2024 alone: $25.5M restaurant-level impairment on 41 stores PLUS $68.3M impairment on Brazil disposal group within disc-ops = $94M of Q4 impairment. Annual goodwill test was performed Q2 2024 (qualitative) — i.e., BEFORE the new CEO arrived and BEFORE the dividend cut, Q4 41-store impairment, and 17% HQ headcount cut all of which post-date the test. PwC critical audit matter is INSURANCE RESERVES, NOT GOODWILL — the auditor did not gate goodwill as a 2024 CAM, which is mildly reassuring but does not preclude a 2025 trigger event (especially under a new CEO who has every incentive to 'kitchen-sink' year 1).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Impairment cadence is accelerating: 41 stores impaired Q4 2024 on top of 36 store closures in FY23 and 73 cumulative closures since FY22. The Q2 2024 qualitative goodwill test pre-dates virtually every adverse fact (CEO change, Q4 impairment, Brazil disposal, dividend cut, traffic acceleration downward) — making it almost certain that the FY25 annual test will be more rigorous and that a 'kitchen-sink' impairment under the new CEO is plausible. The framework should anticipate forward goodwill / trade-name impairment risk even though the FY24 10-K shows no impairment of those assets.

rfm_tuples.R: 'In April 2024, the Company purchased the remaining 0.1 million shares of common stock from the 2024 Share Repurchase Program.' 'The 2024 Share Repurchase Program will expire on August 13, 2025.' 'We did not repurchase any shares of our outstanding common stock during the thirteen weeks ended December 29, 2024.' 'As of December 29, 2024, we had $96.8 million of remaining share repurchase authorization.' From Q1'25 10-Q (5/8/2025): 'We did not repurchase any of our outstanding common stock during the thirteen weeks ended March 30, 2025.' From 8-K 5/5/2025: CEO Spanos bought 118,000 shares at $8.63 (open-market purchase, Code P) on 3/5/2025; SVP/CAO Pace and SVP Graff also acquired smaller blocks via vesting.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B insider-vs-calendar: cross-reference (a) capital-action timing — company STOPPED buying when price collapsed despite $96.8M remaining authorization — with (b) Spanos's 3/5/2025 open-market PURCHASE of 118K shares at $8.63 (~$1.02M). This is the rare contrarian signal: the new CEO put real money in at the trough.
rfm_tuples.M_value: CEO Spanos open-market buy 3/5/2025: 118,000 shares × $8.63 = $1.018M. This occurred 7 days after the FY24 10-K filing (2/26/2025) — i.e., AFTER the bad-news disclosure but inside the open trading window. This is a personal purchase by the new CEO, not a grant. Concurrently, all other insider activity in the relevant window was either RSU vesting + tax withholding (Code M/F at $11.84) or a single small sale by new Outback President Hafner (9,555 shares at $8.32 on 3/4/2025, likely tax-related from prior compensatory grants).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The new CEO's seven-figure open-market purchase at $8.63 is a meaningful counter-signal to the overall distress picture and the framework should weight it. It is the kind of insider action that argues against the most adverse interpretations (further immediate impairment, hidden covenant breach, going-concern risk). It does NOT, however, change the operating reality (traffic decline, dividend cut, C-suite churn) — it merely suggests the new CEO believes the trough has been seen at <$9. From a pure honesty-alpha standpoint, this is honest skin-in-the-game and earns a PASS on this tuple.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Senior Secured Credit Facility matures on September 19, 2029 and replaced our prior senior secured financing of up to $1.0 billion ... TNLR not to exceed 4.50 to 1.00.' 'The 2025 Notes, which mature on May 1, 2025, have been classified as long-term, reflecting the Company's intent and ability to refinance these notes through borrowings on its existing revolving credit facility.' Q1'25 10-Q (footnote 1): 'On May 1, 2025, the 2025 Notes were settled primarily using borrowings from the revolving credit facility.' As of 3/30/2025: revolver balance $600M, total credit facilities $920.7M, available unused $583.7M.
rfm_tuples.f: Capital-structure / debt-wall analysis. (i) The 2025 Notes ($20.7M residual) refinanced into revolver — no maturity wall before April 2029 (2029 Notes $300M) and Sept 2029 (revolver). (ii) New Sept 2024 credit agreement extended runway. (iii) TNLR covenant 4.50x — test cushion. (iv) Brazil sale used to pay down revolver.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Total debt 3/30/2025: $920.7M (revolver $600M + 2029 Notes $300M + residual 2025 Notes $20.7M). Cash $57.7M. Available revolver capacity $583.7M. No bullet maturity for ~4 years. Brazil sale proceeds ($103.9M Dec 2024 + ~$108M expected Dec 2025) directed to revolver paydown. FY24 Adjusted EBITDA = $139.8M op income + $175.6M D&A + ~$10M adjustments ≈ $325M; net debt $1.030B - $70M cash = $960M, implying TNLR ~3.0x — comfortable cushion to 4.50x covenant. Interest cost: 2029 Notes 5.13% + revolver Term SOFR+225bps ≈ 6.22% blend on the variable portion.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Capital structure is NOT the immediate distress vector despite the operating deterioration. The Sept 2024 refinancing (extended to 2029) and the Brazil paydown have effectively removed the near-term debt wall. TNLR cushion ~1.5 turns. This is one area where the distress narrative does NOT apply — the company has a multi-year runway to fix operations or be acquired. This is actually a mild positive in the R/f/M framework: the disclosure is accurate AND the underlying reality is reasonable.

rfm_tuples.R: Claim evolution check between FY24 10-K (filed 2/26/2025) and Q1 FY25 10-Q (filed 5/8/2025). 10-K narrative: 'we remain focused on driving healthy traffic in our existing restaurants' and 'expected liquidity sources are adequate.' 10-Q narrative repeats the same language verbatim while disclosing: (a) Outback Q1 comp -1.3% (deteriorating from -1.2% FY24), (b) Bonefish Q1 comp -4.0% (deteriorating from -3.2% FY24), (c) Bonefish Q1 traffic -9.4% (deteriorating from -7.1% FY24), (d) restaurant-level margin 13.9% vs 15.4% prior-year Q1 (-150bps), (e) severance + restructuring costs $6.1M, (f) FX forward contract costs $2.3M, (g) cash dropped from $70M to $57.7M.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B claim_evolution between 10-K and pre-cutoff 10-Q — the framework's strongest 'lying' tell. Test whether the 10-K's optimistic 'simplify the agenda' / 'traffic improvement' / 'asset-light' framing survives Q1 print 70 days later.
rfm_tuples.M_value: 10-K (2/26/2025) leaned heavily on 'focused on driving healthy traffic in our existing restaurants' as a forward-looking pillar. Q1'25 10-Q (5/8/2025): Outback (the 60%+ revenue brand) deteriorated 10bps; Bonefish deteriorated 80bps with traffic accelerating downward another 230bps (-7.1% → -9.4%). Carrabba's (+1.4%) and Fleming's (+5.1%) improved but these are smaller brands. Restaurant-level margin compressed another 150bps despite the 17% HQ headcount cut. Cash declined $12M in a single quarter. Severance + FX costs of $8.4M cumulative. The Q1 10-Q is signed by the Chief Accounting Officer, not the CFO.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The 70-day claim evolution from 10-K to 10-Q is unambiguously negative on the operating side: (a) the two biggest brands (Outback + Bonefish = ~60-65% of company sales) BOTH deteriorated; (b) restaurant-level margin compressed sharply despite cost cuts; (c) the 'traffic-improvement' narrative pillar is functionally falsified in Q1 (combined U.S. traffic still -3.9% with Bonefish -9.4%). The fact that the Q1 10-Q is signed by the CAO rather than CFO is a minor anomaly worth noting. This is the strongest single Mode-B signal in the file.

rfm_tuples.R: 'On February 20, 2025, Bloomin' Brands, Inc. (the Company) announced that ... it is implementing a workforce reduction at its Restaurant Support Center in Tampa, Florida. The reduction will impact approximately 100 employees ... or about 17% of the Restaurant Support Center team members ... The Company currently estimates that it will incur charges of approximately $7.5 million in aggregate pre-tax costs ... the Company expects that these workforce reductions, coupled with other recent administrative changes, will deliver annualized cost savings of approximately $22 million.' Concurrent with FY24 10-K filing.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-A confirmation (8-K exists and quantifies) + Mode-B economic test: $22M annualized savings against $250M U.S. segment operating income (down from $378M YoY) is ~9% of segment profit. Is this enough to offset the operating deterioration? Compare to incremental P&L pressure: FY24 op margin compressed 330bps (3.5% vs 6.8%) on $3.95B revenue ≈ $130M of EBIT erosion. $22M offsets ~17% of that erosion.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Workforce reduction (~100 people, 17% of corporate) + $7.5M one-time charge + $22M annualized savings. Per Q1'25 10-Q, $6.1M of severance / transformational costs were already recognized in Q1. The 'realignment' also coincides with Lissette Gonzalez moving from Chief Supply Chain Officer to Chief Commercial Officer (no replacement on supply chain disclosed) and Kelia Bazile promoted to Carrabba's President from VP of Operations at Bonefish. The release explicitly cites 'ongoing challenging industry trends' and 'high priority growth opportunities.'
rfm_tuples.interpretation: A 17% corporate headcount cut, taken in the same week as the FY24 10-K filing and ~6 months into the new CEO's tenure, is a clear distress signal (this size of cut is not 'fine-tuning'). The $22M annualized savings is helpful but absorbs only ~17% of the YoY EBIT erosion — and the savings come with execution risk (loss of institutional knowledge at the corporate office during a turnaround). Combined with the dividend cut announced the same week, this is a textbook 'two-handed defensive move' that the framework should treat as MODERATE-to-SEVERE underdelivery on the FY24 'asset-light, drive long-term shareholder value' narrative.

supplemental_signals.auditor_history: PwC since 1998 (27-year tenure). Critical audit matter for FY24 was INSURANCE RESERVES — notably NOT goodwill/intangibles despite a $25.5M Q4 restaurant impairment and a $68.3M Brazil disposal impairment. This is mildly reassuring on near-term goodwill impairment risk but does not preclude FY25 reassessment under new CEO.
supplemental_signals.ceo_transition: Mike Spanos (60) — ex-Delta COO (June 2023-Aug 2024), ex-Six Flags CEO (Nov 2019-Nov 2021), ex-PepsiCo (25+ years incl. CEO Asia/MENA). NO direct restaurant operations background. Effective 9/3/2024. Open-market PURCHASE of 118,000 shares at $8.63 on 3/5/2025 = ~$1.02M personal investment (strong skin-in-the-game contra-signal).
supplemental_signals.cfo_transition: W. Michael Healy CFO since April 2024 (came from internal supply-chain rotation, not finance career path); prior role Bonefish Grill President. Tenure at FY24 10-K filing: ~10 months. Q1 2025 10-Q signed by SVP/CAO Philip Pace, NOT by Healy (minor sub-cert anomaly).
supplemental_signals.dividend_cut: Quarterly dividend cut from $0.24 → $0.15 (37.5% reduction) declared Feb 2025. Annual run-rate from $0.96 → $0.60. Roughly $33-34M annual cash preservation.
supplemental_signals.workforce_reduction: 17% Tampa HQ headcount cut (~100 employees) announced 2/20/2025 — $7.5M one-time, $22M annualized savings. Coincides with new operating-model rollout under Spanos.
supplemental_signals.buyback_asymmetry: $220M ASR at $27.13 in Q1 2024 = 71% of full-year buybacks at peak prices. Zero buybacks in Q4 2024 and Q1 2025 (at $8-15 range) despite $96.8M remaining authorization. Classic asymmetric capital-allocation error. CEO Spanos's personal purchase at $8.63 is the contrarian counter-signal.
supplemental_signals.brazil_divestiture: Sold 67% of Brazil business (the only growth segment) to Vinci Partners for ~$225M USD ($103.9M Q4'24 + $108M expected Dec 2025). Retained 33% with 2028 put/call. New franchise royalty rates 'on the low end of international franchisee range' (below historical 5% intercompany). Functionally a forced de-leveraging dressed as 'simplification.'
supplemental_signals.credit_structure: Sept 2024 new $1.2B revolver extended to Sept 2029. 2029 Notes $300M (5.125%). 2025 Notes residual $20.7M settled May 1, 2025 via revolver. TNLR ~3.0x vs 4.50x covenant (~1.5 turn cushion). No bullet maturity until April 2029 — this is the one bright spot.
supplemental_signals.comp_sales_trajectory: FY24 U.S. combined -1.1% (traffic -4.4%, check +3.3%); FY23 U.S. combined +1.4%. By brand FY24: Outback -1.2%, Carrabba's 0.0%, Bonefish -3.2%, Fleming's +0.2%. Q1'25: Outback -1.3% (worse), Bonefish -4.0% (worse), Carrabba's +1.4% (improved), Fleming's +5.1% (improved). Bonefish Q1'25 traffic -9.4% — brand in run-off.
supplemental_signals.impairment_trajectory: Provision for impaired assets: $6.0M (FY22) → $33.6M (FY23) → $64.3M (FY24). Q4'24: $25.5M on 41 stores + $68.3M on Brazil disposal group. Goodwill $213M and trade names $414M unchanged — annual qualitative test was Q2'24 BEFORE all adverse FY24 H2 events.
supplemental_signals.stockholders_equity: Total stockholders equity $139.4M (POSITIVE, not deficit) at FY24 — accumulated deficit $(925.8)M offset by APIC $1,273M. Down from $412M at FY23 — equity halved in one year. Stockholders equity 4.1% of total liabilities & equity (highly levered).

summary: BLMN at the 2025-05-15 cutoff is a classic late-cycle, leveraged-franchisor casual-dining DISTRESS story with one important counter-signal. Negative side: (1) all four brand-comps traffic-negative with Bonefish in run-off (Q1'25 traffic -9.4%); (2) Brazil divestiture is forced de-leveraging dressed as 'asset-light' (sold the only growing unit to repay revolver); (3) dividend cut 37.5% + 17% HQ headcount cut announced same week as the 10-K — two defensive moves the framework treats as red flags; (4) $266M FY24 buyback at $26.38 average vs $9 cutoff price = classic asymmetric capital allocation; (5) full C-suite rotation in 12 months with new CEO from outside restaurants (Delta/Six Flags/PepsiCo); (6) Q1'25 10-Q signed by CAO not CFO. Positive side: (a) PwC CAM is insurance reserves, not goodwill; (b) new credit agreement extends maturity wall to 2029 with comfortable TNLR cushion; (c) CEO Spanos made a $1M+ open-market purchase at $8.63 on 3/5/2025 — the strongest insider contra-signal. Verdict: SHORT-tier under the honesty-alpha framework — the disclosures are technically compliant but the narrative pillars ('drive healthy traffic,' 'asset-light,' 'long-term shareholder value through dividends and buybacks') are falsified by the Q1'25 print and by the dividend cut. The CEO buy at the trough argues against the most catastrophic outcomes but does not prevent a -10 to -25% additional drawdown as the operating reality continues to deteriorate.
